Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "The subtitle file for the Harbor Lights concert began as a practical favor. Mara Venn, the venue’s production coordinator, had asked Eli Rook to prepare captions for the local archive after the band agreed to let the evening be filmed. Eli had worked on short documentaries, but never on a full concert with a changing stage, improvised introductions, and nearly two hours of music. He arrived before the doors opened with a laptop, a small audio recorder, and a printed set list that had already been marked up in pencil.

The recording took place at the Orpheum Hall on October 18. Harbor Lights played beneath a row of amber lamps, with the audience close enough to hear the band members speak to one another between songs. The camera feed included the stage microphones but not the room microphone, so the loudest applause came through clearly while some comments from the balcony were indistinct. Eli made a separate note of those moments rather than filling in words he could not hear. In the first export, he marked the uncertain audience line as “[unintelligible]” and attached a timecode for review.

Mara sent him the approved set list the next morning. It contained fourteen songs, but the band had played “Paper Moons” between the ninth and tenth listed tracks. The singer, Lio Hart, introduced it as a song they had not performed in several years. Eli checked the audio against the list and added the title in the correct position, noting that the performance order differed from the printed program. The set list remained useful for spelling names and titles, but it could not serve as a transcript of everything that happened onstage.

1. The first review focused on names and recurring terms. The violinist, Nessa Vale, had been identified in the program as “Nessa Vail,” and the venue’s archive staff confirmed the spelling with her before Eli changed the captions. The band’s custom instrument, called a glassbow, appeared several times in the spoken introductions. Eli kept the lowercase spelling used by the band’s website and added it to his working glossary so that the captioning software would not replace it with “glass bow.” He also preserved the capitalization of “North Pier,” the name of a song, even when it appeared in a sentence.

The second review concerned timing. The first version used automatic speech recognition to create a rough transcript, and its captions sometimes stayed on screen after the speaker had stopped. Eli shortened those intervals while keeping each line readable at the concert’s pace. He avoided splitting a performer’s name from the rest of the sentence and kept brief exchanges together when the screen had room. During a fast introduction, the singer said, “This one belongs to everyone who missed the last ferry.” The software rendered “ferry” as “fairy,” a mistake Eli caught by listening again and checking the venue’s transit map.

Mara asked whether the quiet spoken passage before “Low Water” should be captioned as a lyric or as dialogue. The passage was not printed in the band’s lyric sheet, and the singer’s delivery was more like a short address than a sung verse. Eli listened to the recording several times. He kept the words in sentence case and did not add a label such as “spoken” because the shift in delivery was audible in the video. When the band repeated a line together, he used the same wording on both occasions rather than trying to distinguish the voices by name.

The archive’s first playback test revealed a technical issue that had not appeared on Eli’s laptop. The subtitle file used a frame rate of 25 frames per second, while the screening copy ran at 24. The difference was small at the start but noticeable near the end, when captions appeared slightly ahead of the lyrics. The projectionist, Tom Reyes, supplied the correct frame-rate information and a new reference export. Eli retimed the captions against that version, then checked the opening, the encore, and several points between them instead of assuming that one corrected timecode would fix the entire file.

At the final review, Mara asked Eli to retain the original spelling of a phrase that sounded unusual: “leave the harbor light on.” A later email from the songwriter confirmed that the singular “light” was intentional, referring to a particular lamp outside the band’s former rehearsal room. Eli kept the phrase as written and recorded the confirmation in the project notes. He did not add that background to the captions because it was not spoken during the concert and would have changed the file from a transcript into an explanation.

The delivered package contained an SRT file, a plain-text transcript, and a short note listing the recording date, venue, runtime, and frame rate. Mara stored the master video and caption files in separate folders, with matching filenames so that staff could locate them without opening each document. The archive planned to show the concert during its winter program, but the file itself was also intended for online access.
